cinematography-1: I wanted exposures short enough to stop a horse in motion, so I learned to count light in the same units on every camera. A stop is a doubling or halving, and the f-number scale and the shutter speeds are both counted in it. Learn to move between the scales without a calculator, because a change of one stop in either place is the same amount of light. Write the scale on a card and count two examples of your own. Once you can count stops you can compare any two settings, and every exposure decision after this is that comparison.

A film camera exposes while a rotating disc is open and moves the next frame in while it is closed, so the angle of the opening sets the exposure time for a given frame rate. The 180 degree shutter is the usual starting point, and it gives the motion blur that audiences take as normal. Work out the shutter speed for 24 and for 25 frames a second at 180 degrees, and then change the angle and see what the blur does. I put a lot of effort into making shutters fast and exact, and you can feel why when you try to freeze a movement with the wrong one.

Once you have chosen your frame rate and shutter angle, brightness has to come from somewhere else: aperture, sensitivity or a neutral density filter. Count the stops between the light you have and the light you want, and pick a filter that removes that many. Do the sum on paper before you put the filter on. If you change the aperture to fix brightness, remember that it also changes the depth of field, so decide which look you are protecting.

Slow motion comes from shooting faster than you play back, so 48 frames a second played at 24 gives half speed. Faster rates also shorten each exposure, so you need more light. Watch for flicker from lights that pulse, and for the skew of rolling shutters when the camera or the subject moves quickly. Test your camera by panning past a vertical line and look at the result. I laid out cameras to catch a sequence step by step, and testing your own gear is the same habit: you want to know what it will do before you rely on it.
cinematography-2: A stills camera that records video brought a new kind of image to many hands, and with it a set of limits you need to know. The first generation of these cameras had small files, short clips and weak sound. Read what the camera could and could not do, and write the three limits that matter for your shoot. I closed the aperture and lit for it, and I did it because I had tested what the lens and the film would give; the habit is to find out the limits before you build a plan on them.

A sensor's size changes the angle of view a lens gives, and the crop factor lets you convert focal lengths between formats. It also changes the depth of field, the noise and the lenses you can use. Work through the numbers in the lesson by hand: take a lens, say its angle on your sensor, and compare it with the same lens on a larger one. Write one sentence on what a bigger sensor changes in your own scene. Then test two lenses on your camera, because some lose quality at certain stops and the label will not tell you.

A picture profile is a set of tone, colour and sharpness choices baked into the file. A standard profile looks good at once but clips shadows and highlights early, while a flat or log profile keeps more but wants more care and more bits. Learn the exposure aids on your camera and what each one tells you about highlights. Shoot the same scene on two profiles and look at the highlights on a screen. Protect the highlights first, since once they are gone you cannot bring them back.

The camera is a good image recorder and a limited sound recorder. Plan sound, support and card space before the day: a microphone you can monitor, a tripod or rig you can trust, and enough card for the takes. Run the pre-shoot check from the lesson from top to bottom, and write what failed. I tested each lens, because a surprise on the day costs more than a test the day before. Fix what the check finds, then check again.
cinematography-3: A lens's focal length fixes the angle of view, and the angle of view decides how space looks. Wide lenses stretch distance and make movement toward the camera feel quick, while long lenses compress space. Estimate the horizontal angle of a few lenses from the sensor width and write down what each does to a face and to a room. I found that I could get depth from a small aperture and the right light, and a lens choice is part of the same decision. Try the same shot on a wide and a long lens, and see where you stand to keep the subject the same size.

Depth of field is the range that looks acceptably sharp, and it depends on aperture, focal length and distance. A T-stop corrects the f-stop for light lost in the lens, which is why cine lenses are marked in T. Use the formula in the lesson to compare two setups on paper, then shoot both. Deep focus was a choice I made with light, film and glass, and shallow focus is the opposite choice. Know which one the scene needs before you open the aperture.

The aspect ratio is the width divided by the height, and it shapes how a frame is composed. Choose it for the scene, then choose shot sizes with the vocabulary from the lesson: wide, medium, close-up, and what each adds. Frame with a clear subject and leave space where the person is looking. Draw three frames for your scene in the ratio you chose, and ask what each one tells the audience that the others do not.

Primes are sharper and faster than most zooms, and zooms let you change the frame without moving. Adapters let you fit lenses to a body, but they can cost you something. Test any lens before you trust it, chart in hand, at the stops you plan to use. I tested each lens because some lose quality at certain stops, and your own test will tell you which to keep for your key shots. Write the result in your notes.
cinematography-4: Colour temperature compares a light with a glowing black body and is measured in kelvins. Daylight and tungsten differ a good deal, and the camera must be told which one it is seeing. Set white balance to match the light, or use a filter, and then check it on a white card. Note the temperature of the lights in your scene before you start. A mismatch is easy to fix in the camera and hard to fix later.

Three-point lighting uses a key, a fill and a back light to model a subject and control the shadows, and a fourth light can light the background. Set the key first, then add fill until the shadows are the depth you want, and count the difference in stops. In the unchained-camera years I worked with lighting that the equipment could hold, and for television I lowered the contrast so the picture held up in the chain. Decide the key to fill ratio for your scene and write it down.

A light has a colour, a level, a direction and a quality. Hard light comes from a small source and casts crisp shadows, and soft light wraps around the subject. Ask where the light in the scene appears to come from, and place your lamps to match. Motivated light has a reason in the world of the scene, such as a window or a lamp. Sketch your set with the motivation for each light, and cut any light you cannot explain.

A meter reads the light and suggests settings, and an incident meter reads what falls on the subject while a reflected meter reads what bounces off. Use the light-level table in the lesson to plan, then check with a meter or the camera's own aids. I built light meters for the work I was doing, because I wanted a number I could trust. Measure your scene, set the exposure, shoot a test and look at it. Adjust one thing at a time.
cinematography-5: The first film cameras were fastened to a tripod head, so the first films were fixed shots. Every move since then needs a support and a reason. Choose a pan, tilt, track or handheld move and say what it adds to the scene. I took the camera off the tripod, and the reason was that the story needed it to move. Pick the support that suits your kit and check that the move can be repeated. A move with no reason is an effect, and the audience will feel it.

The 180 degree rule keeps the camera on one side of the line between two characters, so the first stays frame right of the second. Draw the line on a plan before you place the camera. Crossing it on purpose can unsettle the audience, so do it only when the story wants it. Check your shots against your plan and watch for continuity of props, eyelines and costume. A diagram on paper saves a day of reshoots.

Coverage means enough positions for the editor to build the scene more than one way: a master, singles, over-the-shoulders and inserts. Write a shot list with the size, the lens, the move and the purpose of each shot. I rehearsed a three-camera set up for four days so that nothing was left to chance. A smaller version of that discipline is a shot list you have walked through with your actors.

On a small shoot one person may operate, pull focus and light, but the jobs still exist. Divide them in writing. Plan the day with times for setting up, rehearsing and shooting, and keep a margin. Think about safety: cables, heights, vehicles and people. I made light meters because I wanted measurements, and the planning habit is the same: write numbers down. At the end of the day, check the schedule against what happened.
cinematography-6: A film gauge is the width of the strip, and each gauge has a frame size, a run time and a typical use. Compare Super 8, 16 mm and 35 mm on those three. Work out the run time from the length of the film and the frame rate. I made film that anyone could load and send back, and the cartridge in the lesson does a lot of the work for you. Choose the gauge that suits the scene and the budget, and say why.

A film stock has a speed and a colour balance, and a filter can correct the mismatch between the stock and the light, at a cost in stops. Reversal film gives a positive image when developed, and negative film gives a negative to be printed or scanned. Work out the exposure change a filter needs from the data sheet. I treated the film itself as the thing that mattered, and you should read the data before you buy it.

Film is exposed now and developed later, so you cannot see the result on set. That makes the test the key habit. Shoot a test roll of your scene, meter it carefully, protect the film from heat and light, and choose a lab. Keep a shot budget so you know how many feet you can spend. Do not skip the test. If the test fails, change one thing and test again.

Film is a different capture medium, not only a look, and it brings costs as well as qualities. List what you gain and what you pay: grain, latitude, cost per foot, delay before you can see. A DSLR can imitate some of the look, but not all of it. Write one sentence on what film gives your scene that digital would not, and one on what it would cost you. Choose with both lists in front of you.
cinematography-7: I built my own camera when only copies of others' films were available, and the lesson is that you understand a machine when you know how it draws the picture. Analog television builds a frame from lines, and an interlaced signal holds two fields, each with half the lines, captured one after the other. Learn what a field is and why NTSC and PAL differ. Draw the lines of a frame on paper and mark which belong to which field.

VHS, Hi8 and Betacam differ in era, in quality and in use. Each tape generation loses some of the signal when you copy it. Compare the formats in a table and say which you would shoot on and which you would only watch. A pixel count tells you little about an analog format, so judge it by what you see. Shoot a short test on a camcorder if you can, and look at the result on a screen.

Telecine moves film to video, and the frame rates do not match. For NTSC, 2:3 pulldown spreads 24 film frames over 30 video frames, and for PAL the film is sped up slightly. Work through the numbers in the lesson by hand. I joined existing machines into new ones, and a transfer is a place where machines meet. Note what each method does to the motion and the sound.

Most film is now scanned and finished digitally, and a hybrid workflow joins the old and the new. Plan ingest, storage, grade and delivery before you shoot. Name every clip with its source, date and take. Match the sources so the film and the digital footage look as if they belong together. Estimate the storage you will need and keep a backup. A plan for the workflow is as much part of the shoot as the camera.
cinematography-cap: The brief is a scene of 60 to 90 seconds, one location, one or two people, with a beginning, a turn and an ending. Write the rubric into your plan, and make the plan complete: shot list, line of action, lighting plan, exposure maths and roll plan. I tripped cameras by wire so that each frame could be compared, and your comparison depends on matching frame rate, shutter angle and framing. Decide what you will match before you shoot.

Work in order. Each step uses a module: exposure, lens, light, movement, film. Shoot the same scene on a digital camera and an analog format. Keep a log of the settings and the takes. Test before the real run, and fix what the test shows. If you cannot match something, note it, because the difference is part of the report.

Ingest the footage, name each clip with its source, date and take, and finish both versions. Compare them honestly: what matched, what did not, and why. I showed the original negative to sceptics, and the report is where you show your evidence. Write what you would change next time, with the numbers to back it. A report that states its limits is more useful than one that claims a win.
